content: Pronation refers to a specific rotational movement in the body. This movement can occur in both the forearm and the foot, involving distinct anatomical joints. In the forearm, pronation is the action of rotating the palm of the hand from an anterior-facing position (palm facing forward) to a posterior-facing position (palm facing backward) when standing in the standard anatomical position. This movement occurs at the radioulnar joint and does not involve any associated motion at the shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint). The muscles responsible for this movement are the pronator quadratus and pronator teres. It is important to distinguish forearm pronation from medial rotation of the shoulder, as the latter can also contribute to a similar change in palm orientation but involves a different joint and movement mechanism. To isolate forearm pronation, one can flex the elbows to 90 degrees with the forearms extended forward and palms facing upward, then rotate the forearms so the palms face downward while keeping the elbows tucked against the trunk. In the foot, pronation describes a movement where the sole of the foot rotates to face more laterally when standing in the anatomical position. A pronated foot is characterized by the inward angling of the heel bone (calcaneus) and a tendency for the arch of the foot to collapse. This is often observed in individuals with knock-knees or excessive foot pronation. During walking or running, this flattening of the arch helps absorb shock when the heel strikes the ground and aids in maintaining balance during the mid-stance phase of gait. Pronation is the opposite of supination, which involves the reverse rotational movements in both the forearm and the foot.
